The keyed answer (the other three follow the French model) is still the best of the four options, so only the explanation needs to change.

Spain (1932 Estatuto del Vino, reworked in 1970) and Italy (DOC, 1963) built their systems on that model. Portugal, whose Douro had been demarcated as early as 1756, rebuilt its Região Demarcada system into DOCs on the same pattern when it joined the EEC in 1986. The European layer then tidied the categories without changing the shape underneath, which is why a student who learns one of the four can read the others quickly.

The examiner's fix, however, has a chronology fault of its own. It says France wrote the pattern "first in 1935" and that Spain built on that model in 1932. claim: Stem: 'Austria's vineyard classification is being written privately before it is written into law'; exp: 'The state's own contribution is the Riedenwein tier, which protects the site name but ranks nothing ... the law only guarantees that the name on the bottle is a real vineyard.'
because: Since the Weinrecht-Sammelverordnung 2023 (August 2023, signed by Agriculture Minister Totschnig), Austrian wine law defines 'Erste Lage' and 'Große Lage'. It reserves both terms for DAC wines from officially classified Rieden, with lower maximum yields and hand harvest. Regional wine committees propose the classifications, and a site can become Große Lage no sooner than five years after Erste Lage. First statutory classifications were expected from the 2025 vintage. The ÖTW model was written into law, so the law now does rank sites and the claim that it ranks nothing is out of date.
fix: Stem: 'Austria's private vineyard classifications preceded the legal one. Which association classified Erste Lage sites along the Danube, and which classifies Erste STK Ried and Grosse STK Ried in Styria?' Replace the last exp sentence with: 'Since the Weinrecht-Sammelverordnung 2023, the law itself provides Erste Lage and Große Lage tiers for DAC wines from officially classified Rieden, proposed by the regional wine committees on the ÖTW model (Große Lage no sooner than five years after Erste Lage; first statutory classifications from the 2025 vintage at the earliest).' Keep the ÖTW and STK answers.
verifyReason: The finding holds. The Weinrecht-Sammelverordnung 2023 added a chapter to Austrian labelling law that creates two legal site tiers, "Erste Lage" and "Große Lage". Both terms are reserved for DAC wines from officially classified Rieden, and only in regions whose DAC already has the three levels Gebietswein, Ortswein and Riedenwein. The classified wines need lower maximum yields and hand harvest. A Ried can become Große Lage no sooner than five years after it became Erste Lage. The Regional Wine Committee starts the process and the National Wine Committee approves it. So the explanation's line that the state's Riedenwein tier "ranks nothing" and that "the law only guarantees that the name on the bottle is a real vineyard" has been out of date since 2023. The keyed answers (ÖTW for the Danube, STK for Styria) are still correct. The original stem is still defensible, because as of the 2024 reporting no region had actually classified any site under the law. The private classifications are still the working ones, and the legal framework is only an offer to the regions. The examiner's fix needs one correction. It says the first statutory classifications come "from the 2025 vintage at the earliest", but the sources only say that no classifications were expected before 2025 (a calendar year, not a vintage). The fix should also say that the National Wine Committee gives final approval.
finalFix: Stem: "Austria's vineyard classifications were written privately before the law made room for one. Which association classifies Erste Lage sites in the Danube regions, and which classifies Erste STK Ried and Grosse STK Ried in Styria?" Keep the accepted answers (ÖTW, STK). Replace the exp from "The state's own contribution..." onward with: "The Riedenwein tier on its own only protects the site name. Since the Weinrecht-Sammelverordnung 2023, however, the law provides two ranked tiers, Erste Lage and Große Lage. They are reserved for DAC wines from officially classified Rieden, and only in regions whose DAC has the Gebietswein, Ortswein and Riedenwein levels. They require lower yields and hand harvest. The Regional Wine Committee proposes the sites and the National Wine Committee approves them, and a Ried can become Große Lage no sooner than five years after it became Erste Lage. No statutory classification was expected before 2025, so in practice the working hierarchy is still the associations' own, largely on the ÖTW model."
